strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question — whether sociodemographic (SD) prompting actually improves alignment of LLM-generated distributions with human survey responses — and does so in a properly distributional setting, correcting the common prior practice of evaluating against a single majority answer per group.

The empirical scope is unusually broad and systematic: 3 survey datasets (US and global), 3 black-box/white-box-compatible distribution elicitation methods, 15 LLMs spanning openness, size, and post-training stage, with ~220,500 generated distributions. This breadth gives the negative results (SD prompting does not consistently help) and positive results (calibration helps in 94.8% of settings, ~16.3% average gain) considerable credibility.

The paper goes beyond aggregate numbers to analyze per-demographic effects, sample-efficiency of supervision (as few as 5 examples suffice), out-of-domain generalization of the calibration, and the effect of post-training stages (base/SFT/DPO/RLVR) — a thoughtful set of research questions.
Practical guidance for practitioners is clearly derived and appropriately hedged (Section 8), and the discussion of essentialization, ethics, and limitations is substantive rather than perfunctory.

Reproducibility is strong: full prompt templates are provided (Tables 12-13), demographic details, all complete result tables in the appendix, and code/data are open-sourced. The metric choice (opinion alignment via 1 - Wasserstein distance, respecting ordinal answer scales) is well justified.

The finding that calibration reduces variance both within and across settings (Figure 2), and that post-trained (uncalibrated) alignment drops while calibrated alignment stays stable (Figure 3), is an interesting and non-obvious observation about LLM distribution miscalibration and exaggeration of inter-group differences.
weaknesses: A central concern is that the calibration results may be substantially an artifact of regression-to-the-mean / variance collapse rather than genuine learning of group-specific distributions. In Tables 1 and 5, calibrated values on WVS converge to a near-constant (~80.3) across almost all models and methods, and calibrated standard deviations drop 1.6-3x, suggesting the regression may be outputting distributions close to the population-average distribution. The paper does not test whether calibrated distributions retain between-group differentiation (e.g., does calibration destroy the SD signal it is supposed to sharpen?), and the claim that 'LLMs exaggerate differences' is asserted from reduced SD without a direct analysis. This needs a stronger control (e.g., a constant/mean-distribution baseline for comparison).

The practical motivation for the method is somewhat circular: supervised calibration requires ground-truth response distributions for the very groups one is trying to predict. The paper partially addresses this via the 5-example and cross-dataset experiments, but the case for real-world usefulness would be stronger if compared against simpler baselines (e.g., shrunken/uniformized distributions, temperature- or mixing-based calibration, or a global calibration curve shared across groups).

Evaluation sets are small: 92 questions total, with 20% test splits and 4-6 examples per individual demographic. Consequently many per-demographic comparisons are not statistically significant (acknowledged by the authors), and headline averages rest on a limited number of test questions. The OQA/WVS subset selection (2 questions per category, for cost reasons) raises representativeness questions.

The core technical contribution (supervised regression to rescale elicited distributions) is simple and application-driven; novelty relative to confidence-calibration literature (Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024; Geng et al., 2024) is moderate, so the paper's value rests mainly on its breadth of empirical findings.

Presentation issues: several typos ('and and', 'degradation varies different SD groups', 'aligment', 'dvelopment'), Figure 4's axes are unreadable at print size, and the bolding/significance scheme in large tables is hard to parse. Some findings (e.g., RQ3/RQ5 interpretations) are speculative and hedged ('might indicate', 'we suspect').

The 'benchmark' framing in the abstract is somewhat overstated given the dataset subsetting and the questions of distribution collapse; as a benchmark it would benefit from stronger baselines and diagnostic measures that separate distribution calibration from group-discrimination.

strengths: The empirical scope is unusually broad: 3 survey datasets (US and global), 3 distribution elicitation methods applicable to both black-box and white-box LLMs, 15 models including a fully open post-training pipeline (OLMo-2 base/SFT/DPO/RLVR), plus out-of-domain generalization and few-shot supervision analyses.

The shift from majority-vote evaluation to distributional evaluation with intra-group disagreement is a well-motivated framing, and the Wasserstein-based opinion alignment metric appropriately handles ordinal answer choices.

The paper is transparent about negative/null results (SD prompting often does not help), includes statistical testing (paired t-test with Bonferroni correction) where feasible, reports all models in the appendix, provides full prompt templates, and includes limitations and ethics statements. The release of a benchmark and open-sourced work aids reproducibility.

The practical guidance sections (Sections 6 and 8) — e.g., that 5 supervised examples often suffice, and that post-training effects are dataset-dependent while calibrated alignment is more stable — are concrete and potentially useful to practitioners simulating survey populations.
weaknesses: The central claim is confounded by a shrinkage effect that is never disentangled. The reported 'calibration reduces variance within and across settings' and 'the choice of any particular model becomes less important' are consistent with regression collapsing LLM distributions toward the marginal human response distribution rather than learning genuine demographic signal. Tables 1, 5, and 8 show suspiciously identical calibrated alignment values (e.g., 80.3 for nearly all models on WVS, and many rows in Table 8 where Vc equals V to 0.1 precision across different models and demographics), suggesting the calibrated distributions converge to a near-identical vector. The paper never measures whether calibrated distributions retain demographic-difference signal (e.g., correlation between predicted and true group-level differences), which is essential to support the framing that LLMs 'exaggerate group differences' and that calibration is beneficial rather than merely a regression-to-the-mean artifact.

The value of supervised calibration for the stated use case is under-argued: if ground-truth response distributions exist for 60-80% of questions, the motivation for LLM prediction is weakened. The 5-example and out-of-domain experiments partially address this, but out-of-domain gains are modest and the paper's own recommendation reverts to collecting in-domain supervision.

Several results are based on very small samples and are reported as trends despite being non-significant (4-6 examples per demographic in RQ3; the RQ4 demographic-degradation analysis explicitly notes no statistically significant differences), which weakens several conclusions, particularly claims about which demographic groups are helped or harmed.

Data and presentation anomalies undermine confidence: unexplained missing entries ('–') in Tables 5 and 9; identical P and S values for Llama-3.2-1B (81.8/81.8, 88.4/88.4) suggesting a possible pipeline issue; a garbled x-axis in Figure 4; and minor but numerous writing errors ('risks and and exercise', 'OLMO', 'degradation varies different SD groups').

Only a single evaluation metric is used, and its saturation behavior (many settings capping near the same value) is not analyzed against an empirical Bayes ceiling imposed by human disagreement; without such analysis, it is unclear how much headroom remains and how to interpret gains near the ceiling.

Methodological novelty is limited — per-answer-choice linear/ridge/lasso/random-forest regression on elicited probabilities is a standard calibration technique — so the contribution rests heavily on the breadth and rigor of the empirical study, which is weakened by the issues above.

The finding that the OLMo-2 base model outperforms its instruct variants on several settings (Table 5) raises the question of whether measured alignment reflects opinion modeling or stylistic response formatting, but this is only briefly speculated upon in Section 7.

strengths: Broad and systematic empirical study: 3 survey datasets (WGM, OQA, WVS), 15 models spanning openness levels and post-training pipelines, 3 distribution elicitation methods, and 2 prompt categories (270 regression settings), yielding a genuinely useful benchmark for distributional opinion alignment.

The supervised calibration idea is simple, well-motivated (LLM distributions may be directionally correct but miscalibrated), and the paper demonstrates it improves alignment in 94.8% of settings while reducing variance across models, datasets, and elicitation methods.

Careful statistical practice: paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction (and ANOVA where triples are compared), reporting of variance, and transparent reporting of negative cases (e.g., the 5.2% of settings where calibration hurts).

Useful secondary analyses: minimal-supervision experiments (1-10 examples suffice), few-shot prompting comparison, per-demographic effects (RQ3), out-of-domain generalization (Appendix A.4), log-probability elicitation comparison (A.2), and post-training effects on a fully open model family (RQ5).

Strong reproducibility: full prompt templates in the appendix, extraction-rate tables (Table 17), explicit train/dev/test splits, and stated plans to open-source; limitations and ethical considerations are candid and thoughtful (essentialization risks, dual use).
Clear framing against prior work: the shift from majority-response evaluation to distributional evaluation with intra-group disagreement is well-argued and connects to pluralistic alignment.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is standard supervised regression (linear/lasso/ridge/random forest) applied per answer choice with renormalization; closely related prior work (Cao et al. 2025; Krsteski et al. 2025; Meister et al. 2025) already covers fine-tuning/rectification and elicitation methods, so the delta is mostly benchmarking plus a simple post-hoc transform.

A missing trivial baseline undermines interpretation: regressing independently per answer choice toward human ground-truth values with only 1-10 training examples needed to converge strongly suggests the regressor largely learns a dataset-level prior (i.e., predicting near the average human response distribution). The suspiciously uniform calibrated scores on WVS (e.g., 80.3 repeated across models and demographics) support this. A baseline that simply outputs the aggregate human marginal distribution, or a 'distance-to-marginal' analysis, is needed to establish that calibration genuinely captures group- and question-specific signal rather than collapsing distributions toward the dataset mean.

Consequently, the headline 16.3% improvement is hard to interpret as distributional alignment gains: the alignment metric rewards any distribution close to ground truth, and a constant near-mean predictor could achieve much of it. The paper's own RQ3 finding that calibration improves some groups and degrades others is consistent with (but not diagnostic of) this collapse.

Question coverage is reduced for cost reasons (all WGM ordinal questions but only 2 questions per category for OQA/WVS), and the per-demographic sample sizes (4-6 examples) are so small that most individual-group significance tests are underpowered, weakening RQ3 conclusions.

Some experimental choices are thin: n=3 or 5 samples for stochastic elicitation methods, fixed temperature 0.7, discarding non-parsing outputs (with substantially reduced extraction rates for some models, e.g., Llama-3.2-1B at ~0%), and MSE as the training objective rather than the evaluation metric — all acknowledged but collectively limiting.

Statistical reporting is occasionally ambiguous (e.g., whether '16.3%' is percentage points or relative improvement), and some claims (e.g., the 'overthinking' hypothesis for Claude) are speculative with limited supporting evidence.

strengths: The empirical scope is genuinely large and systematic: 3 survey datasets, 15 models spanning open-source to API-only, 3 distribution elicitation methods, 2 prompt categories, plus CoT, few-shot, and post-training analyses, giving a useful benchmark-style picture of the distributional alignment landscape.

Statistical rigor is above average for this line of work: paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction, explicit significance marking in the main tables, and repeated random subsampling for the low-resource experiments (Section 6).

The central empirical findings are interesting and consistent: SD prompting does not reliably improve distributional alignment, while simple supervised calibration does, with high per-question sample efficiency (1-10 examples) and reduced variance across models/methods/datasets.

The paper is transparent about failure modes: refusal/parse-failure rates are reported (Table 17), degraded groups are shown, ethical considerations and limitations (essentialization, adversarial use) are thoughtfully discussed.
Reproducibility is well supported: full prompt templates, dataset/demographic specification, open-sourcing, and out-of-domain generalization experiments in the appendix.
The framing toward distributions rather than majority answers is well-motivated by the pluralistic-alignment and intra-group-disagreement literature, and the related work coverage is thorough.
weaknesses: The most decisive concern: the paper lacks a trivial baseline of predicting the dataset-level marginal human distribution for every question and group. Tables 7, 8, and 10 show calibrated alignments converging to nearly constant values per dataset (e.g., WVS VC ~= 80.3 for almost all demographics and models), which strongly suggests the regression largely collapses distributions toward the global human marginal. If so, reported gains may partly reflect removing LLM signal rather than learning question/group-specific alignment, and the claim of improved alignment with 'diverse population groups' would need re-examination. This baseline is essential to interpret the 16.3% average improvement.

Relatedly, the 'variance reduction' result is double-edged: lower variance across settings (Figure 2) is presented as a benefit, but it is also exactly what a collapse-to-marginal solution would produce. The paper does not disentangle genuine calibration from distributional shrinkage, and the suggestion that LLMs 'exaggerate differences between groups' is asserted rather than established.

Methodological novelty is modest. Supervised post-hoc correction of LLM distributions toward human response distributions is close to Cao et al. (2025), Krsteski et al. (2025), and Meister et al. (2025); the contribution is largely the application of simple regression (linear/lasso/ridge/random forest) at scale rather than a new technique, and the paper could better articulate what is scientifically new beyond the empirical map.

The evidence base is thin at the question level: only 92 questions total (38 and 40 for OQA/WVS, just 2 per category), with an 80/10/10 split leaving ~9 test questions per dataset. The headline 16.3% improvement rests on a small test set, and per-demographic evaluations use only 4-6 examples, so most group-level differences are non-significant (acknowledged but this limits RQ3's conclusions).

Training a separate regression model per dataset-LLM-elicitation-prompt setting (270 models) on the same dataset it is evaluated on raises concerns about how much of the gain is dataset-specific distribution fitting; the out-of-domain appendix results help, but the main claims are in-domain.

The calibration objective (MSE on answer-choice values) differs from the evaluation metric (Wasserstein-based alignment), and the discrepancy is not analyzed; it is unclear whether results would hold or improve under aligned objectives.

Some analyses feel incomplete or under-interpreted: the CoT 'overthinking' explanation is speculative with only anecdotal evidence, the income findings in Section 5.2 are hand-waved, and the claim that smaller Llama models' refusal rates drive variance is not isolated experimentally.

Given the title and framing ('Improving the Distributional Alignment of LLMs'), the paper under-addresses the possibility that calibration is improving aggregate similarity at the cost of the pluralistic, group-distinguishing signal the motivation emphasizes.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly framed: the critique of prior work assuming a single majority answer per sociodemographic group (the ecological fallacy) is well grounded, and the shift to evaluating distributional alignment with the Wasserstein-based opinion alignment metric is appropriate for ordinal survey responses.

The empirical scope is unusually broad and systematic: 3 datasets (WGM, OQA, WVS), 15 models spanning multiple families, openness levels, and post-training regimes, 3 distribution-elicitation methods, base vs. SD prompts, and additional variations (CoT, few-shot), yielding ~220,500 distributions.

The paper follows a clear RQ structure and answers each RQ with specific evidence, including honest reporting of negative or mixed results (e.g., SD prompting does not consistently improve alignment; calibration degrades alignment for ~5% of settings and for some demographic groups).

Reproducibility is addressed seriously: full prompt templates, training/evaluation splits, hyperparameter search details, significance testing (paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction), a report of distribution-extraction failure rates per model, and a stated commitment to open-sourcing the work.

The analysis of data efficiency (MSE converging with 1-10 supervised examples), few-shot prompting comparison, out-of-domain generalization across datasets, and post-training effects on the fully open OLMo-2 family adds genuine value beyond the headline calibration result.
The limitations and ethical considerations sections are substantive and self-aware, including the risk of essentializing sociodemographic categories and dual-use concerns.
weaknesses: The most significant concern: the paper lacks a trivial baseline that predicts the mean human training distribution for each question (or dataset-level marginal) without using the LLM at all. In the results tables, calibrated values for many models collapse to nearly identical numbers (e.g., 80.3 for many models on WVS), suggesting the learned regression may often be close to a constant function that outputs the dataset-level marginal. If so, a large share of the reported 16.3% average improvement could be obtained by such a no-LLM baseline, which would substantially weaken the central claim that 'LLM distributions are uncalibrated and can be supervised into alignment.' The authors note that the choice of model matters less after calibration, but do not confront this confound directly.

Relatedly, the training procedure regresses each answer-choice value independently toward the supervised targets, which by construction shrinks toward the mean and reduces variance; claims that 'LLMs exaggerate differences between groups' and that calibration 'mitigates stereotyping' need stronger evidence than variance reduction alone, since regression-to-the-mean mechanically produces the same signature.

The per-demographic analysis (RQ3) has very small samples (4-6 questions per demographic), so few differences are statistically significant; conclusions about which groups benefit from calibration are largely descriptive.

The few-shot comparison (Section 6.2) uses only 3 of the 10 random samples used elsewhere, with limited justification, and does not explore stronger prompting-based alternatives (e.g., larger k, distribution-verbalizing few-shot), which weakens the claim that calibration is preferable to supervision-free approaches.

Coverage is only a subset of questions per dataset (e.g., 2 per category from OQA/WVS) due to cost; it is not clear how representative the sampled questions are of each survey, and there is no discussion of possible selection bias.

Novelty of the core method is modest: supervised regression from model outputs to human targets is a standard technique; the contribution is primarily the systematic empirical study and benchmark, which is valuable but the headline framing ('supervised calibration') could be more carefully positioned relative to marginal-correction baselines.
